Sophia Antipolis, France

Université du Mans
Le Mans, France
Anthony.Larcher@univ-lemans.fr
Abstract
Self-supervised speech models such as WavLM achieve strong spoofing detection performance, yet which layers encode the most spoof-relevant information and what acoustic properties they capture remain opaque.
We present a layer-wise interpretability study of WavLM using the ASVspoof 5 database, combining three complementary analyses:
(i) per-layer linear probing with attack-level evaluation across speech synthesis, voice conversion, and adversarial attacks;
(ii) a canonical correlation analysis (CCA) linking layer representations to spoofing-relevant acoustic features; (iii) an exhaustive grid search over layer subsets showing that use of five layers outperforms full thirteen-layer pooling.
CCA analysis reveals that, while most acoustic features peak in alignment with mid-layers and then decay, voice quality measures jitter, shimmer, and the harmonics-to-noise ratio show the opposite trend, with correlation increasing toward later layers.
Embedding visualisations reveal that deeper layers capture a continuous acoustic similarity among attacks rather than discrete categories, suggesting these layers encode fundamental synthesis artifacts rather than attack-specific signatures.

I Introduction
Self-supervised learning (SSL) front-ends have become the backbone of modern spoofing countermeasures (CMs) and presentation attack detection (PAD) solutions, achieving state-of-the-art performance for ASVspoof benchmarks [1, 2].
However, these models remain opaque; it is unclear which layers encode spoof-relevant information, how layer behaviour varies across attack types, and whether the learned representations can be linked to interpretable acoustic properties.
Herein lie the goals of our work reported in this paper.
Recent work shows that spoofing countermeasures can exploit spurious cues and learning shortcuts [3], e.g. those linked to non-speech duration. This further motivates analyses that ground model behaviour in meaningful acoustic properties.
Among a plethora of available and popular alternative SSL models, we focus on WavLM [4] which incorporates a denoising pre-training objective that exposes the model to noisy and overlapped speech.
Because WavLM is trained to recover masked targets for a designated main speaker in noisy/overlapped mixtures, its denoising objective encourages representations that preserve speaker-related information and remain stable under acoustic distortions.
We report an investigation performed using the most recent ASVspoof 5 database [5].
It provides a diverse set of bona fide speech utterances together with a set of spoofed/deepfake attacks generated using text-to-speech (TTS), voice conversion (VC), and adversarial perturbation methods, all treated with varied codecs and recording conditions [1].
Its crowdsourced nature and the diversity of the data and acoustic conditions make it an ideal test bed for interpretability-driven analysis.
We address three research questions:
1. 
Which WavLM layers carry the most discriminative bona fide-spoof information?
2. 
Does the detection of different attack families (TTS, VC, adversarial) depend upon the capture of information at different layer depths?
3. 
What interpretable acoustic properties do WavLM layers encode, and how do these relate to known spoofing markers?
The contributions of the work reported in this paper include:
Attack-aware layer characterisation - We provide a comprehensive analysis of how spoofing discriminability varies with representation depth and attack types, revealing strong layer-attack interactions and showing that mid-to-deep layers carry the most reliable bonafide/spoof cues under most conditions. 
Layer subset search - We show that an optimally chosen compact layer subset can outperform standard all-layer pooling with a linear backend, providing a practical efficiency gain.
CCA-based acoustic grounding - We link layer representations to interpretable spoofing-relevant acoustic cues by computing projection-weighted canonical correlation analysis (PWCCA) showing a shift in representation geometry helping explain why certain layers behave differently and when they fail. t-SNE visualisation corroborates this: representations transition from discrete attack clusters (mid-layers) to a continuous horseshoe manifold (deep layers).
Fig. 1: Overview of the analysis pipeline. Top: WavLM produces frame‑level layer representations; each layer is summarised by mean+std pooling to a 1536‑D utterance vector. Bottom left (blue): PWCCA pipeline, PCA (1536→50) and correlation between pooled layer vectors and handcrafted acoustic features, producing layer vs feature heatmaps. Bottom right (pink): per‑layer linear probing, yielding per‑layer EER and per‑attack EER heatmaps.
II Related Work
II-A Spoofing CMs and SSL front-ends
Neural spoofing countermeasures (CMs) now span a broad range of back-ends, including graph-attention architectures such as AASIST, conformer-based anti-spoofing classifiers, and fused/ensemble systems [6, 7, 1, 8, 9]. In recent ASVspoof 5 submissions, these back-ends are frequently paired with SSL front-ends such as wav2vec 2.0 and WavLM, often together with augmentation (e.g., RawBoost) and score/model fusion strategies [1, 10, 11, 4, 12, 8].
II-B Layer-wise analysis of SSL models
Previous layer-wise studies of SSL speech representations [13, 14] show that early layers capture local acoustic features while late layers encode more abstract content and speaker information. In the context of spoofing detection, studies have explored SSL front ends [8, 10, 9], but primarily to optimize detection performance. More recently, Xiao et al. [15] proposed layer-wise decision fusion for fake audio detection, demonstrating that per-layer decisions outperform feature-level fusion.
Representation analysis tools such as singular vector canonical correlation analysis (SVCCA) [16] and projection-weighted canonical correlation analysis (PWCCA) [17] provide quantitative similarity measures between representations. However, these tools have not yet been applied to interpret what spoofing-relevant information individual layers encode in an attack-dependent manner.
II-C Acoustic cues for spoofing detection
Specific acoustic features like jitter, shimmer, and the harmonic-to-noise ratio measures of vocal fold micro-perturbations are known markers of spoofed speech; TTS vocoders produce unnaturally smooth or irregular voice quality patterns [18].
Formant trajectories have been shown to expose voice conversion artifacts; generative models struggle to replicate fine-grained articulatory detail [19, 20].
Spectral features such as sub-band centroids and flux have also been studied; spectral discontinuities from frame-level synthesis leave detectable traces in these measures [21].
While none of these features alone match the detection performance of modern SSL-based systems, they offer the advantage of direct interpretability. The shift toward self-supervised models has improved accuracy but moved the field further from understanding what information drives detection. Whether SSL representations internally encode the same acoustic properties as these handcrafted features explicitly measure remains unexplored. Our CCA analysis addresses this question by directly measuring the alignment between WavLM layer representations and these spoofing-relevant acoustic features.
These findings motivate our choice of CCA target features.
III Methodology
An illustration of our analysis pipeline is shown in Figure 1.
It comprises two components:
(i) per-layer linear probing for discriminability assessment (bottom right, pink block);
(ii) canonical correlation analysis (CCA) which is applied between layer representations and handcrafted acoustic features so as to ground representations in interpretable spoofing-relevant utterance characteristics (bottom left, blue block).
We describe both in the following after a description of the dataset and attack taxonomy and our use of WavLM representations.
III-A Dataset and attack taxonomy
All work reported in this paper was performed using the ASVspoof 5 database [5], using the Track 1 protocol for spoofing/deepfake detection and with the standard train, development (dev) and evaluation (eval) partition splits [22].
The train set contains attacks A01--A08 (GlowTTS, GradTTS, FastPitch, VITS variants), the dev set A09--A16 (ToucanTTS, Tacotron2, StarGANv2-VC, YourTTS, VAE-GAN, and others), and the eval set A17--A32 (including ZMM-TTS, MaryTTS, DiffVC, among others, and adversarial methods such as Malafide and Malacopula).
For analysis, we group the set of 32 attacks into three families, specifically those generated using TTS and VC and those augmented11

III-B WavLM representations and linear probing
We use the WavLM Base model [4] as a frozen feature extractor extracting representations from all layers (L0–L12).
Unlike wav2vec2.0 [11], which is trained solely with a contrastive objective using clean speech, WavLM incorporates an additional denoising objective that exposes the model to noisy and overlapped speech during pre-training.
This design makes WavLM particularly relevant to our analysis, since spoof detection depends on both acoustic distortions and speaker-related properties.
We use the Base variant rather than the Large model for computational efficiency and because its 13-layer architecture provides a tractable setting for layer-wise analysis while still achieving competitive performance for many speech-related tasks.
Since all WavLM layers produce 768-dimensional frame representations, direct layer-wise comparison is straightforward.
For each layer, we compute mean and standard deviation pooling over the time frame axis, yielding two 768-dimensional statistics which are concatenated into a single 1536-dimensional utterance-level vector suitable for classification.
Using training data only, we learn distinct linear classifiers using the representations extracted from each layer to distinguish bona fide from spoofed utterances.
We select the best model according to that which produces the lowest equal error rate (EER) for the development set and report EERs for all bona fide and spoofed data in both the development and evaluation sets.
This approach provides a transparent measure of layer-wise discriminability without the use of complex back-ends obscuring interpretation.
III-C CCA-based acoustic feature analysis
To ground WavLM representations in interpretable acoustic properties, we estimate the correlation between the representations of each layer and a set of 17 handcrafted acoustic features organised into four categories:
• 
Voice quality (3): jitter, shimmer and the harmonic-to-noise ratio (HNR), measures of vocal fold micro-perturbations known to be distorted by TTS vocoders [18].
• 
Prosodic (4): F0 mean, F0 standard deviation, energy mean, onset strength.
• 
Spectral (6): MFCC mean, spectral centroid, spectral roll-off, ZCR, spectral entropy, spectral flux, general signal descriptors used in CM [21].
• 
Harmonic/formant (4): harmonic ratio, F1 mean, F2 mean, F3 mean, formant trajectories expose voice conversion artifacts [19, 20].
We use canonical correlation analysis (CCA) to measure how well each WavLM layer’s representations align with a set of handcrafted acoustic features [17]. CCA identifies linear projections of two variable sets that are maximally correlated. Here, these correspond to the pooled layer representation 𝐱∈ℝd1\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}} and the acoustic feature vector 𝐲∈ℝd2\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{2}}, yielding coefficients ρ1≥ρ2≥⋯≥ρk\rho_{1}\geq\rho_{2}\geq\cdots\geq\rho_{k}, where k=min⁡(d1,d2)k=\min(d_{1},d_{2}).
Standard CCA can be sensitive to directions with low variance.
We therefore adopt projection-weighted CCA (PWCCA) [17], which computes a weighted mean of canonical correlations:
PWCCA=∑i=1kαi​ρi∑i=1kαi\text{PWCCA}=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{k}\alpha_{i}\rho_{i}}{\sum_{i=1}^{k}\alpha_{i}}

where αi\alpha_{i} is the sum of absolute projection weights onto the ii-th canonical direction, giving greater weight to directions that capture greater variance in the original representation.
CCA requires the number of samples to exceed the dimensionality of both inputs; following [17], we reduce layer representations to 50 dimensions via principal component analysis (PCA) prior to computing PWCCA.
We compute correlations between each 1536-dimensional layer representation and the 17 acoustic features matrix.
Canonical correlations are weighted by projection magnitudes and symmetrised by averaging in both directions.
To report per-feature correlations (Fig. 3), we compute the squared correlation between each individual feature and the first canonical variate of the layer representation. Analyses use the train+dev splits only, with the eval set reserved for final reporting. For computational efficiency, we randomly sample up to 5000 speaker-balanced utterances per attack group. This sample size comfortably exceeds the reduced dimensionality and supports reliable correlation estimates.
IV Results
We report results for both development and evaluation sets.
The study of results for both sets allows us to examine whether layer-wise patterns observed for more familiar attacks generalise to unseen conditions, and to identify where generalisation fails.
Fig. 2: Per-attack EER (%) across WavLM layers for the dev (A09–A16) and eval (A17–A32) splits, with overall per-layer EER for each set shown in the two rightmost columns. Green indicates low EER (easy detection), whereas red indicates high EER (hard detection). The vertical black line separates dev and eval attacks.
IV-A Per-layer probing
Per-layer EERs from frozen WavLM representations with linear classifiers are shown in Fig. 2 for both dev and eval sets.
For both sets, performance generally improves with depth up to L11 resulting in the lowest dev EER of 3.33% and the lowest eval EER of 6.07%.
EERs for L12 are higher, showing a loss of discriminative information.
A visualisation of EER results for each layer and each attack is shown in Figure 2.
Several patterns emerge.
For the dev set, near-zero EERs (dark green colours) are achieved for some TTS attacks (A09, A10, A14 and A16) from mid layers onward.
Notably, the EER for A12 (unit selection) is higher for early layers but drops sharply after L6 (from up to ≈\approx80% for early layers dropping to ≈\approx5% for late layers), suggesting that deeper representations capture artifacts that shallow layers miss.
For all other attacks in the dev set, and with only few exceptions, EERs are higher than 5% for all layers.
For the eval set, most attacks follow a similar pattern of decreasing EER with depth. However, for three TTS attacks, A22 (ToucanTTS variant), A24 (ASR-based TTS), and A28 (pre-trained YourTTS), we observe the opposite trend: EERs exceed ∼\sim30% in later layers, higher than that for mid-layers. What distinguishes these attacks from others that become easier to detect with depth is explored further in Section IV-B.
For attacks augmented with Malafide [23] (A18, A20, A23) and Malacopula [24] (A27, A30–32) adversarial filtering, EERs are consistently high (EER>>20%) for all layers, with either flat or inverted layer trends.
This is expected since adversarial filters are optimised to suppress detectable artifacts, whether by maximising CM scores (Malafide) or matching target speaker embeddings (Malacopula).
The uniform failure across all layers suggests that adversarial optimisation successfully removes detectable artifacts regardless of representation depth, exposing a fundamental limitation of artifact-based detection.
IV-B CCA analysis
PWCCA results are illustrated by a heatmap shown in Figure 3.
Colours indicate the correlation between representations extracted from each WavLM layer and individual acoustic features. Two distinct patterns emerge.
Correlation Peak Around L7- Most acoustic features follow a consistent pattern: correlation increases from L0, peaks at around L7, and then decays toward L12. Spectral features show the strongest mid-layer alignment, with that for the spectral centroid reaching 0.96 at L7, followed by MFCC mean (0.92) and spectral roll-off (0.91). Prosodic features (F0, energy) follow the same trend with slightly lower peak values. Formant features (F1–F3) show the weakest correlations overall (peaks of 0.70–0.78), suggesting that formant information is less accessible from WavLM representations than spectral or prosodic properties. This pattern mirrors the acoustic-to-abstract transitions reported previously for SSL models [13]: mid-layers encode signal-level properties while later layers encode more abstract representations.
Uniform Increase in Correlation- In contrast, jitter, shimmer, and HNR show monotonically increasing correlation with layer depth. Jitter rises from 0.52 (L0) to 0.89 (L12), shimmer from 0.53 to 0.90, and HNR from 0.55 to 0.94. These features measure micro-perturbations in pitch period, amplitude, and harmonic structure properties that vocoders and TTS systems are known to distort  [18].
These two patterns help explain the probing results. The EER improvements from early to mid-layers coincide with stronger spectral and prosodic encoding, while the further gains at late layers are driven by increasing voice quality sensitivity — even as spectral alignment decays.
Voice quality correlation is greatest for L12, yet EERs are slightly worse than for L11 (7.3% vs. 6.07%), suggesting a greater balance between retained spectral information and voice quality sensitivity.
Fig. 3: PWCCA correlation between WavLM layers and individual acoustic features. Most features peak at mid-layers and decay, while voice quality measures (jitter, shimmer, HNR) increase with depth.
IV-C Layer subset search
The per-layer results show clear variation in discriminability across layers, raising the question of whether a compact subset can match or outperform full-layer pooling. To test this, we perform an exhaustive grid search over all ∑k=113(13k)=8191\sum_{k=1}^{13}\binom{13}{k}=8191 possible layer combinations. For each subset of kk layers, we concatenate the corresponding 1536-dimensional representations into a single k×1536k\times 1536-dimensional vector and train a linear probe. Subsets are selected on dev only; eval is used once for final reporting.
Table I compares the top subsets against the full 13-layer baseline (19 968-dimensional input). The best 5-layer subset (L7–9–10–11–12) achieves 6.1% eval EER, outperforming the full baseline (8.08%). All top subsets concentrate in the L6–L12 range. This is consistent with the CCA findings in Section IV-B: layers beyond L6 exhibit the strongest alignment with spoofing-relevant acoustic properties, particularly the voice quality features (jitter, shimmer, HNR) whose correlation increases monotonically with depth. Early layers, which encode primarily low-level spectral information with weaker discriminative relevance, do not contribute complementary information in the linear pooling setting.

IV-D t-SNE Visualisation
Figure 4 shows t-SNE projections of WavLM representations at three depths for the eval splits.
For L1, attacks form overlapping clusters with no clear separation.
For L6, discrete attack-specific clusters appear and the model appears to distinguish attacks (coloured points) from bona fide utterances (black points).
For L11, attacks form a continuous horseshoe arc with bona fide samples lying at one end of the shoe.
We observed this pattern to be consistent across multiple t-SNE random seeds and perplexity settings (20, 30, 50).
The horseshoe arc is often associated with data organized along a dominant continuous latent dimension [25].
This observation aligns with the PWCCA result: mid-layers show stronger correlation with categorical spectral features (forming discrete clusters), while late layers correlate more strongly with voice quality features (jitter, shimmer, HNR).
The shift from discrete to continuous organisation suggests that late layers organise attacks along a gradient of vocal naturalness rather than by categorical attack identity.
Fig. 4: t-SNE visualisation of WavLM representations at layers 1, 6, and 11. Representations transition from overlapping clusters (L1) to discrete attack-specific groupings (L6) to a continuous horseshoe manifold (L11).
V Discussion
The results offer insights into how WavLM encodes information relevant to spoofing detection.
Voice quality and layer depth -
The most striking finding from the CCA analysis is that voice quality features (jitter, shimmer, HNR) show increasing correlation with late layers, in contrast to the decay observed for spectral and prosodic features.
This difference may reflect the WavLM denoising objective during pre-training which exposes the model to degraded and overlapped speech.
Being tasked with predicting masked tokens from corrupt input, the model may develop sensitivity to fine-grained signals.
These layers achieve the lowest EER suggesting a direct link: the ability to encode voice quality patterns translates to spoofing discriminability, since vocoders are known to distort these properties [18].
Attack-specific layer signatures -
The per-attack heatmap (Fig. 2) reveals that detection performance is not uniformly distributed across layers.
Some attacks (A09, A10, A14, A16) are detected from mid-layers onward, while detection of A12 (unit selection) is better for late layers.
On the other hand A22, A24 and A28 evade detection at late layers despite being detectable at mid-layers.
This implies that different synthesis methods leave artifacts at different levels of abstraction: conventional TTS systems may introduce voice quality distortions caught by late layers, while high-quality neural TTS systems trained on greater quantities of data may produce natural voice quality but leave spectral or prosodic artifacts that are captured by mid layer representations.
These attack-specific layer signatures have practical implications: a fixed single-layer will at some point fail on certain attack families, motivating multi-layer or adaptive layer selection strategies.
Adversarial robustness -
The uniform failure across all layers for adversarial attacks (Malafide, Malacopula) highlights a fundamental limitation of artifact-based detection. These methods are explicitly optimised to remove detectable cues, and our results confirm they succeed regardless of layer depth. This suggests that robustness to adversarial attacks may require defenses beyond representation learning, such as adversarial training or detection methods that do not rely solely on acoustic artifacts.
Limitations -
Linear probes capture only linearly accessible information. We study a single SSL model (WavLM Base), and other architectures may show different layer-wise behaviour. Our CCA analysis also assumes linear relationships between representations and acoustic features. In addition, all experiments are conducted on ASVspoof 5, so the reported trends may not transfer unchanged to other corpora, real-world recordings, or unseen attack families. Finally, our acoustic feature set is not exhaustive.
VI Conclusions
We present a layer-wise interpretability study of WavLM for spoof detection using the ASVspoof 5 database combining linear probing, CCA-based acoustic grounding and layer subset search.
Mid-to-late layers (L9–L11) are most discriminative, and a compact 5-layer subset outperforms full 13-layer pooling.
CCA reveals that voice quality features (jitter, shimmer, HNR) correlate increasingly with late layers, the same layers that achieve the most reliable detection, while spectral and prosodic features peak at mid-layers and decay.
t-SNE visualisations corroborate these observations, showing that late layers organise attacks along a continuous gradient of vocal naturalness.
These findings provide an interpretable grounding for SSL-based layer selection and highlight the challenge posed by adversarial attacks that are designed to evade detection.
Future work should examine whether these layer-wise trends remain stable across other corpora, real-world conditions, and unseen attack families.

Framing Spatial Hearing within the Free Energy Principle: A Hierarchical Model of Perceptual Learning
Roberto Barumerli
Affiliation: Dyson School of Design Engineering, Imperial College London, UK
Nils Meyer-Kahlen
Affiliation: Dyson School of Design Engineering, Imperial College London, UK
Affiliation: Dept. of Information and Communications Engineering, Aalto University, Finland
E-mail r.barumerli@imperial.ac.uk
Lorenzo Picinali
Affiliation: Dyson School of Design Engineering, Imperial College London, UK
Abstract
Spatial hearing relies on dynamic internal representations to decode spatial information from ever-changing acoustic conditions. A fundamental example is sound localisation, where listeners infer the direction of an invisible sound. Bayesian inference provides a computational account of such a localisation process; however, modelling efforts are largely limited to static listening scenarios. Instead, the free energy principle (FEP) describes perception, learning, and action as joint minimisation of variational free energy (VFE), providing a principled framework to account for dynamic conditions. Here, we take a first step toward applying the FEP to spatial hearing. We characterise how listeners’ beliefs evolve across trials, in which they estimated sound direction and received subsequent visual feedback on each trial.
Listeners are described by a hierarchical generative model where visual feedback drives gradient descent on VFE, updating beliefs over three independent quantities: lateral and polar localisation precisions and hemifield disambiguation. The model captures individual learning trajectories and reveals components with different dynamics: lateral precision improves, as does hemifield disambiguation, consistent with increased sensitivity of the auditory pathway in decoding vertical direction. Notably, polar precision also increases, most for listeners with the lowest initial precision, suggesting that the observed vertical improvement is driven by both hemifield disambiguation and polar precision. This work establishes spatial hearing as a tractable domain for FEP and motivates future closed-loop experiments with full action-perception cycles.
Introduction. Understanding how the auditory system decodes spatial information is a central challenge in hearing research, yet computational accounts largely focus on static scenarios [11, 3], leaving its dynamic, experience-dependent nature under-explored [4]. Auditory spatial perception is inherently plastic [16] and localisation involves both perception and action [13], making the FEP, a unified computational account of perception, learning, and action [8, 15], a natural framework.
Localisation improves across trials with visual feedback [10], yet no mechanistic account exists of how individual beliefs evolve trial by trial.
Here, we use the FEP [5] to model perceptual learning as belief revision, decomposing localisation improvement into three components with distinct timescales, validated on behavioural data from [10].
Problem formulation. On each trial ii, the listener estimates the direction of an invisible sound source 𝝋t\bm{\varphi}_{t} and produces a pointing response 𝝋r\bm{\varphi}_{r}, followed by visual feedback at 𝝋t\bm{\varphi}_{t}. Directions are expressed in interaural-polar coordinates 𝝋=(α,β)\bm{\varphi}=(\alpha,\beta)  [14], separating the contributions of auditory cues to behavioural error (Fig. 1): the lateral angle α\alpha, informed by interaural time and level differences, defines the cone of confusion, within which the polar angle β\beta is decoded from spectral-shape cues [13]. With uniform priors on 𝝋r\bm{\varphi}_{r} and 𝝋t\bm{\varphi}_{t}, the listener model factorises as p⁡(𝝋r|𝝋t,𝜽)=p⁡(αr|αt,𝜽)​p​(βr|αr,βt,𝜽)p(\bm{\varphi}_{r}|\bm{\varphi}_{t},\bm{\theta})=p(\alpha_{r}|\alpha_{t},\bm{\theta})\,p(\beta_{r}|\alpha_{r},\beta_{t},\bm{\theta}) where 𝜽\bm{\theta} captures the listener’s beliefs about lateral and polar precisions, and hemifield disambiguation (i.e., front–back confusions [13]).
We employ a parametric formulation to preserve differentiability within FEP. The lateral component is a von Mises distribution with location αt\alpha_{t} and concentration κL\kappa_{L} (i.e., lateral precision). The polar component is a two-component von Mises mixture with concentration κP\kappa_{P} (i.e., polar precision), locations βt\beta_{t} and π−βt\pi-\beta_{t} (i.e., correct and incorrect hemifields) and hemifield weight ww; κP\kappa_{P} is scaled by cos2⁡(αr)\cos^{2}(\alpha_{r}), reflecting the reduced relevance of spectral cues at lateral extremes, where the interaural cone collapses (Fig. 1) [14, 12].
Belief revision follows from minimising variational free energy ℱ\mathcal{F} with respect to 𝜽=(κL,κP,w)\bm{\theta}=(\kappa_{L},\kappa_{P},w). With a flat prior and Laplace approximation [6], ℱ\mathcal{F} reduces to −log⁡p⁡(𝝋r|𝝋t,𝜽)-\log p(\bm{\varphi}_{r}|\bm{\varphi}_{t},\bm{\theta}), so belief revision amounts to online likelihood ascent: a deliberately minimal instance of the FEP, covering perception and learning but not action (Fig. 2). Each belief takes a natural-gradient step [2] after every trial, scaled by the inverse Fisher information to update components living on different scales consistently (problem formulation available in Appendix A.1). Updates are sequential, producing a trajectory that batch optimisation cannot recover.
Per subject (N = 5), learning rates (ηL,ηP,ηw)(\eta_{L},\eta_{P},\eta_{w}) were estimated by maximum likelihood [1], and 𝜽0\bm{\theta}_{0} from the baseline block [10] (Appendix A.2).
Results and Discussion. The model captures group-average trajectories (R2=0.75,0.83,0.79R^{2}=0.75,0.83,0.79 for lateral, polar and hemifield errors, Fig. 3, top). Individual parameter trajectories (Fig. 3, bottom) differ across components: κL\kappa_{L} rises for most subjects; κP\kappa_{P} rises, proportionally more for lower baseline κP\kappa_{P}; ww increases steadily (median ηL,ηP,ηw=0.010,0.015,0.014\eta_{L},\eta_{P},\eta_{w}=0.010,0.015,0.014; Appendix A.3).
These distinct trajectories are consistent with previously reported mechanisms, including sensorimotor recalibration [10], stable spectral cue-to-direction mappings acquired through natural listening [7], and increased sensitivity to altered spectral cues [9].
Notably, behavioural polar dispersion decreases and κP\kappa_{P} rises under the cos2\cos^{2} weighting: the improvement seen in aggregate statistics stems from hemifield disambiguation and sharper polar precision (Fig. 3, middle column).
Our approach has limitations: a small cohort and a perception-only loop in which pointing is a read-out and feedback is external. Two extensions would cast spatial hearing as full active inference: informative priors on 𝜽\bm{\theta}, yielding posterior uncertainty on κP\kappa_{P}, and head movements as policies, resolving hemifield ambiguity by action rather than by learning.

B. Synthetic-injection training
Labelled ENF data are scarce, so the detector is trained on
synthesised examples anchored to a small quantity of real
recordings. A grid's drift is modelled as an Ornstein-
Uhlenbeck process fitted to real mains measurements, and a
continuous ENF drawn from it is injected into a hum-free
carrier: clean speech for the audio channel, and rolling-shutter
video whose own flicker has first been suppressed for the
optical channel. The optical injection places the modulation at
each row's true exposure time, so extraction inverts the same
geometry that generated it (Fig. 4, Table I).

AcousticAgent: A Floorplan-Centric Simulation Platform for Distributed Multi-Room Speech Processing
Zhiqi Ai
Han Cheng
Shiyi Mu
Yongjin Zhou
Shugong Xu
††thanks: *Corresponding authors
Abstract
Existing acoustic simulation tools either generate room impulse responses (RIRs) efficiently in parameterized rooms or rely on preconstructed three-dimensional scenes, making it difficult to build large numbers of editable residential multi-room environments. We present AcousticAgent, a floorplan-centric acoustic simulation platform that converts structured floorplans into editable, acoustically connected multi-room scenes. AcousticAgent jointly models room geometry and connectivity, furniture, materials, sound sources, and microphone configurations. A scene-oriented Acoustic Materials Database maps semantic elements to acoustic parameters, while a floorplan-aware hybrid geometrical-acoustics solver generates multichannel RIRs and reverberant audio. The platform also supports directional and moving sources, distributed microphones, and VLM-assisted scene construction from floorplan images and text. Using AcousticAgent, we construct FP-RIR, a dataset covering 15,376 residential floorplans with diverse room topologies, propagation conditions, and source–receiver configurations. We validate its acoustic fidelity against real-world measurements and evaluate whole-home source localization, speech enhancement, and far-field speech processing under single-device and distributed microphone settings. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of floorplan-aware modeling for large-scale residential acoustic simulation and the benefits of distributed spatial processing in multi-room environments. AcousticAgent and FP-RIR provide scalable and configurable resources for developing and evaluating residential speech systems.

1 Introduction
Residential speech interfaces often operate under far-field and cross-room conditions, where sound sources and microphones may be far apart, obstructed by furniture, or separated by intervening walls. The received signal therefore varies with room topology, source–receiver geometry, inter-room connectivity, and the acoustic properties of surrounding surfaces [31, 36]. This spatial variability makes it difficult for a single microphone to provide uniform coverage throughout a home. Distributed microphone systems alleviate this limitation by combining spatially complementary observations and have been studied for source localization, distributed beamforming, speech enhancement, and multi-device speech processing [4, 15, 12, 7].
Developing and evaluating such systems requires acoustic data spanning diverse residential layouts, material properties, and source–microphone configurations. Measured corpora preserve real propagation effects, but each recording campaign is tied to a finite set of physical spaces and device deployments; broader coverage requires additional deployment and data collection [30, 28, 13]. Room impulse response (RIR) simulation provides a scalable means of varying these factors, but its practical scalability depends not only on propagation computation, but also on how efficiently acoustic scenes can be specified. Parameterized simulators often require room geometry, materials, and device positions to be explicitly defined, which becomes cumbersome when many irregular multi-room layouts must be instantiated. Mesh-based platforms can represent richer three-dimensional environments, but rely on preconstructed scene assets [10, 32, 5, 19]. Large-scale residential simulation therefore calls for a scene representation that is both acoustically meaningful and easy to construct, edit, and vary.
Structured floorplans provide a compact representation of room geometry, semantics, and connectivity. They can be parsed from raster images or generated from structural constraints and natural-language descriptions without requiring complete three-dimensional assets [17, 8, 1, 11, 22]. To form a computational acoustic scene, however, they must be augmented with furniture, acoustic materials, source and microphone configurations, and models of within-room and cross-room propagation. Although floorplans are widely used for visual parsing, layout generation, and embodied scene construction, their use as the core representation for large-scale acoustic simulation remains underexplored.
To address this gap, we present AcousticAgent, a floorplan-centric platform for multi-room acoustic simulation. AcousticAgent converts structured floorplans into editable, acoustically connected scenes that jointly represent room geometry and connectivity, furniture, materials, sound sources, and microphone configurations. A scene-oriented Acoustic Materials Database maps semantic scene elements to acoustic properties, while a floorplan-aware hybrid geometrical-acoustics solver models within-room and cross-room sound propagation to generate multichannel RIRs and reverberant audio. The platform further supports directional and moving sources, microphone arrays, distributed microphones, and VLM-assisted scene construction from floorplan images and textual descriptions.
Using AcousticAgent, we construct FP-RIR, a large-scale dataset spanning 15,376 residential floorplans with diverse room topologies, within-room and cross-room propagation conditions, and flexible source–receiver and distributed-microphone layouts. We validate the simulated acoustic characteristics against measured RIRs and establish a distributed multi-room speech-processing benchmark covering whole-home source localization, speech enhancement, and far-field speech processing under single-device and distributed microphone settings.
Our main contributions are summarized as follows:
• 
Floorplan-centric multi-room acoustic simulation.
We introduce AcousticAgent, which converts structured floorplans into editable, acoustically connected multi-room scenes through semantic acoustic-material assignment and floorplan-aware geometrical-acoustics simulation.
• 
Large-scale FP-RIR dataset.
We construct FP-RIR spanning 15,376 residential floorplans with diverse room topologies, within-room and cross-room propagation conditions, and flexible source–receiver and distributed-microphone layouts.
• 
Distributed multi-room speech-processing benchmark.
We establish a benchmark for whole-home source localization, speech enhancement, and far-field speech processing under single-device and distributed microphone settings.
2 Related Work
2.1 Acoustic Simulation and RIR Generation
Indoor acoustic simulation generates room impulse responses (RIRs) or
reverberant audio by modeling sound propagation according to scene geometry,
material properties, and source–receiver configurations. Existing approaches
are commonly categorized into wave-based and geometrical-acoustics methods
 [34, 31]. Wave-based methods, such as
finite-element and finite-difference methods, solve the acoustic wave equation
and accurately capture interference, diffraction, and room modes, but their
computational cost increases rapidly with scene size and frequency range
 [34]. Geometrical-acoustics methods approximate
propagation using geometric paths and provide efficient alternatives through
image-source methods, ray tracing, and path tracing
 [3, 31, 36].
Existing simulation tools mainly target either efficient parameterized room
simulation or detailed three-dimensional scene rendering. RIR-Generator and
gpuRIR provide image-source-based simulation for parameterized rooms, while
FRAM-RIR and Pyroomacoustics support efficient multichannel RIR generation and
microphone-array processing [14, 10, 23, 32]. For more general environments, Steam Audio,
SoundSpaces 2.0, and SonicSim enable geometry-based acoustic rendering over
three-dimensional scene representations
 [35, 5, 19]. These systems provide
powerful acoustic rendering capabilities, but constructing large numbers of
editable residential multi-room scenes remains challenging, particularly when
layouts, materials, and source–receiver configurations need to be varied
systematically.
2.2 Floorplan Representation and Scene Construction
Structured floorplans compactly encode architectural geometry, room semantics, and spatial connectivity. CubiCasa5K supports architectural-element parsing from annotated raster floorplans, while FloorplanVLM converts raster images into structured vector representations  [17, 22]. ResPlan provides large-scale residential layouts with explicit semantic and connectivity information  [1]. ArchiText and ProcTHOR further explore layout generation and procedural residential scene construction  [11, 8]. While structured layouts are widely used in visual understanding and embodied environment construction, acoustic simulation additionally requires material properties, source and microphone configurations, and cross-room propagation modeling. Their use as a central representation for large-scale acoustic scene construction remains underexplored.
Figure 1: Overview of AcousticAgent.
AcousticAgent transforms floorplan images, natural-language descriptions,
or sampled residential layouts into editable multi-room acoustic scenes
with explicit geometry, connectivity, furniture, and semantic material
parameters. Its floorplan-aware hybrid solver combines deterministic
propagation, Monte Carlo ray tracing, and parametric late reverberation to
generate multichannel RIRs for static or moving sources and flexible
microphone configurations.
2.3 Distributed Multi-Room Speech Processing
Distributed microphone systems exploit spatially separated observations for sound source localization, beamforming, speech enhancement, and speech separation [4, 15, 12, 37]. Recent work further combines multi-device acoustic front ends with downstream tasks such as keyword spotting, speaker verification, and automatic speech recognition  [39, 21, 20, 7]. Measured corpora are essential for evaluating real-world propagation and device effects. DIRHA-English provides distant-speech recordings in domestic environments, FFSVC 2020 targets far-field speaker verification with distributed microphone arrays, and Libri-adhoc40 contains synchronized recordings from 40 microphones in a real office  [30, 28, 13]. However, such datasets cover only a limited number of environments, room topologies, and sensor layouts. Large-scale controllable simulation is therefore needed to complement real recordings and support systematic evaluation across diverse residential floorplans and microphone configurations.
3 AcousticAgent
As shown in Fig. 1, AcousticAgent transforms
residential floorplans into editable, acoustically connected multi-room scenes
for multichannel room impulse response (RIR) generation. Its key design is to
decouple reusable scene content—including geometry, connectivity, furniture,
and materials—from dynamic source and receiver configurations. Once a scene
has been constructed, it can be reused across different source positions,
trajectories, directivities, and microphone layouts. AcousticAgent comprises
four components: floorplan-centric acoustic scene construction, semantic
material parameterization, floorplan-aware acoustic simulation, and flexible
source and microphone configurations.
3.1 Floorplan-Centric Acoustic Scene Construction
AcousticAgent accepts structured floorplans, raster floorplan images,
natural-language descriptions, or layouts sampled from a residential
floorplan corpus. Image- and text-based inputs may be processed with optional
LLM/VLM assistance, after which all inputs are normalized into the same
explicit and editable scene representation.

3.3 Floorplan-Aware Acoustic Simulation
Given the scene geometry, material parameters, and a source–receiver

Using AcousticAgent, we construct FP-RIR, a floorplan-based multichannel RIR dataset for far-field and multi-room speech processing. FP-RIR contains 15,376 validated residential floorplans from ResPlan [1], comprising 120,150 rooms and 107,595 open interior portals. For each floorplan, six-band acoustic materials are assigned according to scene semantics, and source and receiver positions are sampled from collision-free regions. For each floorplan, we generate two within-room monophonic configurations and up to three cross-room configurations recorded by four-channel circular microphone arrays. Cross-room source–receiver pairs cover different topological distances and are retained only when they are connected through valid sequences of open portals.
As shown in Fig. 2, FP-RIR covers residential floorplans containing 2–14 rooms, with a median of 7 rooms. The broadband R​T60RT_{60} estimated from the generated RIRs has a median of 0.84 s and a 95th percentile of 1.48 s, reflecting acoustic diversity arising from variations in room geometry, material assignment, and cross-room connectivity.

4.3 Downstream Benefits of Distributed Front Ends
Experimental setup. We reuse the test scenes, source-level-calibrated mixtures, microphone
deployments, and MWF front ends from the whole-home speech enhancement
experiment. The enhanced signals are evaluated using frozen Whisper Tiny and
Whisper Small models for ASR [29], and frozen CAM++ [38] and ERes2Net [6] models for speaker
verification. We use 1,000 LibriSpeech [26] test-clean utterances for ASR and
construct 1,000 VoxCeleb1 [24] verification trials with clean enrollment.
Results.
Distributed arrays achieve the lowest WER for both ASR models
(Table 3), reducing WER by 71.7–78.1%
relative to the fixed living-room array. GCC-FP also provides substantial
improvements under the smaller four-channel budget, showing that
floorplan-aware microphone selection benefits downstream recognition.
For speaker verification, both distributed configurations substantially
reduce EER and minDCF compared with the fixed array
(Table 4). Distributed arrays obtain the
best overall results, indicating that spatially distributed capture improves
both speech recognition and speaker verification without downstream-model
adaptation.
5 Conclusion
In this paper, we present AcousticAgent, a floorplan-centric platform for constructing editable multi-room acoustic scenes, together with FP-RIR, a large-scale multichannel RIR dataset. AcousticAgent combines semantic material parameterization, portal-aware propagation, Monte Carlo ray tracing, and parametric late reverberation under flexible source and microphone configurations. Validation against measured RIRs demonstrates reliable estimation of DRR and reverberation characteristics. Distributed benchmarks show that one microphone per room can approach the source-room localization performance of array-per-room systems with fewer channels, while distributed arrays provide the most consistent performance in speech enhancement and downstream ASR and speaker verification. Together, AcousticAgent and FP-RIR provide a scalable and reproducible testbed for residential distributed speech processing. Future work will investigate measured multi-room calibration, asynchronous devices, dynamic portal states, and moving speakers.

1.7 VLM-Assisted Custom Floorplan Construction
Beyond the indexed residential corpus, AcousticAgent supports custom acoustic
scenes derived from user-provided floorplan images. An external online
vision–language model (VLM) receives the image together with a
schema-constrained prompt and returns a structured description of room
polygons, walls, doors, windows, scale, and room connectivity. The user may
calibrate the metric scale before submitting this description to
AcousticAgent. The system then validates polygon topology, normalizes the
coordinate system, resolves shared boundaries, and converts valid openings
between adjacent rooms into acoustic portals.
The validated layout is lifted into a three-dimensional scene using the
specified room height. Source and receiver positions, frequency-dependent
semantic materials, and optional furniture can subsequently be sampled or
edited through the same interface used for corpus floorplans. Furniture may
be placed manually or generated by the semantic auto-placement module under
room-type, boundary-clearance, portal-clearance, and compactness constraints.
The resulting geometry is passed without modification to the floorplan-aware
solver described above.
Importantly, the VLM acts only as a geometric parser. It neither predicts
acoustic coefficients nor synthesizes the RIR. Material sampling, direct and
portal-mediated propagation, diffraction, Monte Carlo reflections, and the
parametric late tail remain deterministic components of AcousticAgent once
the structured scene and random seeds are fixed. This separation makes the
custom-scene interface auditable while allowing a broad range of floorplan
styles to be simulated without manual geometric reconstruction.

1.8 RIR and Auralization Examples
Static scene.
Figure 7 shows the complete transformation from
a dry source to a static far-field observation. The RIR contains a sparse
onset followed by a dense decaying tail. Relative to the dry spectrogram, the
wet signal exhibits broadened harmonic ridges and residual energy between
speech events, reflecting frequency-dependent attenuation and temporal
smearing by the cross-room propagation path and reverberant field.
Dynamic scene.
The keyframe stack in Fig. 8 exposes changes
that a single static RIR cannot represent. As the receiver approaches the
source, the early response and late-field level evolve continuously. The wet
spectrogram consequently becomes progressively stronger while preserving
smooth transitions between frames. This interpolation is identical to the
dynamic auralization procedure used by the Web workbench and avoids abrupt
switching between independently simulated RIRs.
Furniture ablation.
Figure 9 isolates the acoustic effect of
furniture from source placement and material randomness. The furnished RIR
decays more rapidly across most of the tail because beds, sofas, rugs, and
other semantic objects introduce additional absorption and scattering area.
The corresponding wet spectrogram contains less persistent inter-event energy
than the unfurnished rendering. This comparison confirms that semantic
objects participate in acoustic simulation rather than serving only as visual
assets.
1.9 Interactive Web Workbench
The Web workbench exposes scene construction and acoustic simulation through a
single synchronized interface. Geometry, FloorPlan, and Custom modes share
the same source, receiver, material, furniture, motion, solver, RIR,
auralization, and API controls. Editing the scene invalidates the previous
result; running the solver updates the path visualization, metrics, RIR, and
rendered audio from one consistent simulation state.
